5. Discussion
These results begin to quantify the differences in data carriers used in 
CCSC. The results ultimately showed that QR codes and NFC chips are 
similar in user experience and time to complete tasks. NFC had slightly 
faster times and a slightly higher user experience than QR codes. Though 
not statistically significant, QR codes and NFC chips also showed 
marginally reduced errors. DPM was the slowest and received the worst 
user experience rating. The difference in testing locations is shown to 
potentially intermediate between the data carrier system and the DVs 
but no further statistically significant effect was detected.
An important difference between these data carrier systems is that 
DPM requires the data to be stored somewhere else (digital or physical) 
and match the marking, QR codes can store a short string and require 
additional data to be stored digitally while NFC chips store data inter­
nally. Both QR codes and NFC necessitate additional reading devices, 
though most smartphones are equipped to read both.
Though existing circular supply chain management work uses re­
views, conceptual models, case studies, and inter-views, explicit gaps 
found are the lack of quantitative re-search (Lahane et al., 2020). This 
research, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, is the first of its kind to 
quantify differences in data carriers for building products. Although this 
was explored in the context of product passports for CCSC, it is appli­
cable for general construction supply chains, circular supply chains, and 
industrialized construction. Using an experimental design to assess the 
effectiveness of different data carriers offers a methodological approach 
for future research in similar domains.
The results of this work supplement existing research on cyber- 
physical-social systems in AEC and construction sup-ply chains that do 
no provide research or justification on the selection of data carriers. 
Although some research develops bespoke RFID solutions Swift et al. 
(2017); Li et al. (2022), this work examines the user-based tradeoffs in 
the radio-based technologies relative to QR codes or traditional DPM. 
Furthermore, the work continues the research on designing the track 
and trace stack for MPs and DPPs Çetin et al. (2021, 2023). It does not 
focus on the content of the passports nor the storage, but on the linkage 
of data to the physical product. The choice and implementation of a data 
carrier for resued construction materials may help to alleviate the 
challenge of a lack of initial product information as identified by 
(Farooque et al., 2019). Ultimately, the work establishes an under­
standing of the role of digital technologies in enabling a CCSC, offering a 
specific perspective on the nexus of sustainability and data 
transparency.
5.1. Cost comparison
For the data carrier devices used, the unit costs and additional capital 
costs for the specific experimental materials are compared in Table 1. 
The cost per unit is composed of the materials used to tag the compo­
nents and store the data. The costs are transformed to USD from the 
original purchase (1 CHF = 1.11 USD at time of writing).
For DPM the cost of the label and the print of the data sheet were 
included, for QR codes it includes the cost of the label and the storage of 
1 MB of data, and for NFC it is the cost of the tag. The minor costs for 
storage of data (0.0001–0.001 USD for 1 MB) were averaged over 
different data storage providers for Switzerland. For all of the technol­
ogies, devices already present in companies like printers or smartphones 
are not accounted for.
The costs for NFC tags vary from 0.10 to 100 USD (Balluff, n.d.), 
depending on the storage and engineering of the encasing (Khattab 
et al., 2017). However, the vinyl sticker tags used are widely available 
and suit this application.
